topic: Skillsync (YC W26): making AI chat sessions portable across agents

key_points: Launch HN thread (2026-09-17, 68 points, 62 comments) is the primary first-party source: founders answer every objection in-thread, so it doubles as the FAQ a review post can quote

Founder (cat-whisperer): conversion is deterministic format translation with no AI involved — 'there's no ai here. Everything is retained including tool calls, reasoning and handed off to the other agent'

Co-founder Narsagna on fidelity limits: 'With longer sessions, the receiving agent sometimes decides to compact it. But the whole transcript still exists and is accessible' — the receiving harness' own context management is the real degradation point, not the translation
Positioning vs markdown work journals (critique from pjm331): a journal is produced from a prompt, so anything the prompt did not ask about is gone; the raw session still has it
Counter-position acknowledged by founder: 'Porting is cheap, since it's just a format conversion. Getting a new session back up to speed from notes usually isn't.'
Direction is one-way today — from a chat/consumer session INTO a coding agent. Merging a colleague's session into an already-open one is explicitly not supported yet
Cross-machine sync exists (SSH to machines, or export run.json and continue it locally); Antigravity, Hermes, pi, OpenClaw and Cursor are named as supported

Real community friction surfaced in-thread: archived Codex/ChatGPT chats were not auto-discovered; user solfox filed issue #52, submitted PR #53, and maintainer merged it the same day (2026-09-17) — public evidence of the open-core contribution loop

Skepticism is part of the record: 'syncing is trivially solved by just telling the agent to keep a work journal in markdown' and a commenter calling the category useless ('either out of the box or 2 prompts away')
Privacy/contact papercut reported live: the email on the Privacy page bounced; founder republished founders@skillsync.com — useful real-world caveat for a review
The open-source core: 'Pandoc for AI chats' — a Rust library, CLI and WASM that converts session transcripts between harnesses; Apache-2.0 licensed
Metrics as of 2026-09-29: 142 stars, 12 forks, 8 contributors, 23 open issues, actively pushed (commits same day: claude_code tool-result UUID fix, Cowork cloud sessions, session lineage)

Adapters with both read AND continue support: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor CLI, Cursor desktop, pi, Campfire, Cowork, Grok CLI, fx, Antigravity. Read-only: Hermes Agent, Amp. Live-account sources (Claude Chat, ChatGPT, Cloud Cowork) are read-only
Conversion is lossy by design when the destination cannot represent a record — README states 'Agent-specific records and unsupported fields can be lost'
Crucially, the destination supplies its own system instructions and tools, and project files must be brought separately — portability covers the conversation, not the environment
CLI surface a review can walk through: list / query / view / crop / export / continue / resume, plus 'txcript mcp' exposing read-only tools for MCP clients
A neutral 'Simple' interchange JSON lets any unadapted agent participate, and txcript export writes it — the interoperable escape hatch
Rust 1.96+ required to build from source; prebuilt binaries for macOS, Linux and Windows
Product surface: macOS desktop app + CLI (skl) + MCP server; tagline 'Your AI sessions made portable across every agent and teammate'
Works-with list on the marketing page: Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw, Grok, Grok Bot, Antigravity, pi, OpenCode, Cursor
Three claims to hold it to: 'Resume any session on your local coding agent, or move it to a different one mid-stream', 'Portable, searchable context', 'Multiagent + multiplayer'
Local-first positioning is explicit: sessions, skills and memory stay on each machine until a member shares them
Free tier for individuals: all local sessions searchable, continue on any agent, personal skill library on every agent, analytics, CLI + MCP server — the paid wall is collaboration, not portability
Pro Teams: shared workspaces, cloud sync, 'self-improvement', up to 10 seats — price is not published, only 'Get started' (Book a demo)
Enterprise: unlimited users/workspaces, custom harness integrations, priority support

Workspace model splits three things teams share: sessions (teammates can read, search, pick up on their own agent), skills (one library installed on every member's agents), and memory (workspace notes/learned skills load into Codex and Claude Code when a session starts)
Pricing-opacity is the main commercial caveat for a buyer-facing review: no public number for Pro or Enterprise
YC W26, Active, Developer Tools, San Francisco; one-line pitch is 'Notion for AI chats'
Founder: Narayana Aaditya Ganeshkumar (Founder/CEO); background claim — helped take an open-source Rust project from zero to 30k+ GitHub stars; focus on engineering/product/organizational psychology
Sells the compounding-context story: because sessions are portable they 'stack up instead of disappearing', so every past session stays searchable and feeds the next agent
States the local-first privacy line and that the core engine txcript is a portable session format no single provider owns
Closest direct alternative (built by yoavfr, who posted it in the same HN thread): converts a session into the target agent's native format and opens it where you left off
Narrower scope — Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode only, macOS only, v0.3.1, Swift, MIT, 10 GitHub stars vs txcript's 142
Differentiator it owns: user control over how much of the conversation to bring (which the Skillsync founder publicly complimented)
Useful as the 'simpler and smaller' comparison point — no team/workspace layer at all
Second open-source alternative, Python: claims migration across 18 harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, Copilot, Antigravity, Vibe, Muse, Qwen, Kimi, Cursor)
118 stars, 10 forks, created 2026-08-17 — younger than txcript and already within striking distance on stars, so the adapter-count race is crowded
Shows the honest competitive frame: the moat is not 'move a session', it is depth of adapter fidelity plus the workspace/team layer around it
PyPI-published (v0.5.0, requires Python 3.11+), local-first cross-harness export/resume for Claude Code, Codex and Hermes
0 stars — included as evidence that this is now a commodity pattern with a very long tail of tiny tools, not a two-player market

Third-party analyst characterization (2026-09-17): classifies Skillsync as open source that 'moves AI coding agent chat sessions between agents, so a team can switch tools without losing the conversation'
Frames the business impact as avoiding lost context and restarted tasks when teams switch AI coding tools — the team-angle framing, not the individual-developer one
Independent confirmation of the 'ffmpeg or pandoc for agent sessions' analogy and of the local-first Mac app + CLI + MCP trio

90% of professional developers used AI coding agents at work at least weekly in May-July 2026, and 68% daily (Developer Ecosystem Survey 2026, 15,000+ professional developers, 10th edition)

Claude Code reached ~39% adoption at work (up from 18% in Jan 2026; 47% in the US), Codex grew ~5x to 16%, GitHub Copilot fell to 21%, Cursor slipped to 12%, OpenCode reached 7% — i.e. developers now run multiple agents side by side, which is precisely the precondition for session portability

"Handoff Debt": context-bearing handoffs between coding agents cut median agent events by 20-59% and cumulative prompt tokens by 42-63% versus a repository-only takeover, across 181 handoff-point tasks and 724 takeover runs per successor model

One developer's measured corpus of 722 sessions / 150,902 model calls / 34.56 billion tokens: 97.05% of billed tokens were cache reads, and under list pricing context handling was 87.8% of cost versus 12.2% for generation — re-reading context cost 4.59x everything the models wrote

Instrumented production compression gateway across Claude Code/Codex and Claude Sonnet/GPT-5: tool-schema filtering removes a fixed ~21K-57K tokens per typical turn and is the only reliably positive lever; file-read compression saves only ~2% of the cached prefix per turn but accumulates quadratically (~3350*N^2 tokens)

MCP directory counts: 20,000+ public MCP servers (MCP.so 21,000+, Glama.ai 23,000+); 67 million local MCP server downloads in April 2026; 72% of surveyed technical leaders expect their MCP usage to increase
MCP market sized at USD 1.20B in 2025 and projected to USD 28.36B by 2035 (US 0.45B -> 10.27B; Europe 0.24B -> 5.16B)

Skillsync is open-core and the contribution loop is real: user-filed issue #52 (archived Codex/ChatGPT chats were invisible to discovery) got PR #53 the same day and was merged by the maintainer on 2026-09-17

Adapter breadth vs the field: txcript 142 stars / 17 harness adapters with 11 supporting both read and continue; closest rival Continuo (Swift, macOS) supports 3 harnesses with 10 stars; session-migrate (Python) claims 18 harnesses with 118 stars; agent-session-bridge has 0 stars

angles: The real problem is not model switching, it is sunk context: a session is an asset you cannot take with you, so choosing an agent early locks in later. Skillsync reframes the agent choice from a bet into a reversible decision.

Deterministic, not generative: the founder's claim that 'there's no ai here' is the single most important architectural fact — no summarizer rewrites your history, which is what makes an audit trail possible. Contrast that with the note-taking/journal approach where a prompt decides what survives.

Where fidelity actually breaks, told honestly: not in the translation but in the receiving agent's own compaction, plus destination-supplied system instructions and tools, plus project files that must be brought separately. 'Portable conversation' is not 'portable environment'.

The handoff-debt payoff with a number attached: arXiv:2606.02875 measures 42-63% fewer cumulative prompt tokens on context-bearing handoffs; set that next to the 97% cache-read share of agent token bills and portability stops looking like convenience and starts looking like cost control.

The crowded-second half of 2026 reality check: Continuo, session-migrate, agent-session-bridge and an open core mean 'move a session' is now a commodity. The defensible layer is fidelity depth plus the team workspace (sessions + skills + memory shared per machine, not uploaded).

Local-first as the trust argument: sessions/skills/memory stay on each machine until a member shares them, and the format itself is the open standard — worth contrasting against cloud-sync-only tools for teams with sensitive repos.

The 2026 multi-agent workflow it enables in practice: brainstorm in a consumer chat on a phone, then continue in Claude Code at the desk while the full reasoning and tool history ride along; and for teams, ship a session to a colleague instead of a summary, so the colleague can see the evidence behind a change.

What to verify before you trust it with real work: what the destination cannot represent and silently drops per the README's own warning, one-way-only limitation (no merge), the read-only vs continue adapter split (Hermes Agent and Amp are read-only), and the private-web-API sources (Claude Chat, ChatGPT, Cloud Cowork) that reuse an app login.

Open-core governance question for a buyer: with Apache-2.0 core and 8 contributors plus 23 open issues, how much of the roadmap is community-driven vs commercial lock-in at the Teams tier — the archived-chats fix pattern is the model, not the exception.
